entries.name: Aspirin
entries.subtitle: Acetylsalicylic acid · NSAID and antiplatelet
entries.summary: One of the oldest and most studied medicines. Used for pain and fever, and at low dose to prevent blood clots in people at high risk.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Pain, fever and inflammation. Low-dose aspirin is used to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke in selected people, only when a doctor advises it.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Permanently blocks the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. This lowers prostaglandins (pain, fever, inflammation) and, in platelets, thromboxane, so blood clots less easily.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Stomach irritation and bleeding, including stomach ulcers. Can trigger breathing problems in some people with asthma.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: Higher bleeding risk with blood thinners such as warfarin, with other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, and with alcohol.

sections.title: Do not use
sections.text: In children or teenagers with a viral illness such as flu or chickenpox, because of the risk of Reye's syndrome.

entries.name: Paracetamol
entries.subtitle: Acetaminophen · pain reliever and fever reducer
entries.summary: A common first choice for pain and fever. Gentle on the stomach, but an overdose can cause serious liver damage.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Mild to moderate pain and fever.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Not fully understood. It is thought to act mainly in the brain, reducing pain signals and fever, with little anti-inflammatory effect.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Taking more than the maximum daily amount can cause severe, sometimes fatal liver damage. Many cold and flu products also contain paracetamol, so doses can add up without noticing.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: Regular heavy alcohol use raises the risk of liver damage. Long-term use may increase the effect of warfarin.

entries.name: Ibuprofen
entries.subtitle: NSAID · anti-inflammatory pain reliever
entries.summary: A widely used anti-inflammatory for pain, fever and swelling.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Pain, fever, and inflammation such as in arthritis, muscle pain and period pain.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Temporarily blocks the COX enzymes, lowering prostaglandins that cause pain, fever and swelling.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Stomach bleeding and ulcers, kidney problems, and a higher risk of heart attack and stroke, especially with long use or high doses. Prescription NSAID labels in the US carry a boxed warning about these risks.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: More bleeding with blood thinners and aspirin. Can weaken some blood pressure medicines and harm the kidneys when combined with them.

sections.title: Pregnancy
sections.text: Usually avoided in later pregnancy unless a doctor advises it.

entries.name: Metformin
entries.subtitle: Biguanide · type 2 diabetes medicine
entries.summary: The usual first medicine for type 2 diabetes, used for more than 60 years.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Lowering blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, together with diet and exercise.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Reduces the amount of sugar the liver releases and helps the body respond better to insulin. It does not usually cause low blood sugar on its own.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Stomach upset and diarrhoea, usually at the start. Long-term use can lower vitamin B12. A rare but serious risk is lactic acidosis, mainly in people with poor kidney function; the US label carries a boxed warning about it.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text: Kidney function should be checked regularly. Doctors may pause it around some X-ray scans that use contrast dye.

entries.name: Amoxicillin
entries.subtitle: Penicillin-type antibiotic
entries.summary: A widely used antibiotic for common bacterial infections.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Bacterial infections such as ear, throat, chest and urinary infections, and as part of treatment for H. pylori stomach infection.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Stops bacteria from building their cell walls, so they burst and die.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Allergic reactions, from rash to rare life-threatening anaphylaxis. People allergic to penicillin should not take it. Diarrhoea is common.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text: Antibiotics do not work against viruses such as colds and flu. Taking them when they aren't needed helps bacteria become resistant.

entries.name: Atorvastatin
entries.subtitle: Statin · cholesterol-lowering medicine
entries.summary: Lowers 'bad' LDL cholesterol and reduces the risk of heart attack and stroke.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Lowering LDL cholesterol and reducing cardiovascular risk in people at higher risk.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Blocks HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Muscle aches; rarely serious muscle breakdown. Liver enzyme changes. Not used in pregnancy.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: Some antibiotics, antifungals and HIV medicines raise its level in the blood and the risk of muscle problems. Large amounts of grapefruit juice can do the same.

entries.name: Amlodipine
entries.subtitle: Calcium channel blocker · blood pressure medicine
entries.summary: A common once-daily medicine for high blood pressure and chest pain (angina).

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: High blood pressure and angina.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Relaxes and widens blood vessels by blocking calcium from entering the muscle cells in their walls.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Ankle swelling, flushing, headache and dizziness.

entries.name: Omeprazole
entries.subtitle: Proton pump inhibitor · stomach acid reducer
entries.summary: Strongly reduces stomach acid. Used for reflux and ulcers.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Acid reflux (GERD), stomach and duodenal ulcers, and as part of treatment for H. pylori infection.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Blocks the 'proton pump' in stomach cells that produces acid.

sections.title: Long-term use
sections.text: Linked to low vitamin B12 and magnesium, a higher risk of some bone fractures, and certain gut infections.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: Can reduce the effect of the blood thinner clopidogrel.

entries.name: Salbutamol
entries.subtitle: Albuterol · short-acting reliever inhaler
entries.summary: The blue 'reliever' inhaler used to quickly open the airways.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Quick relief of wheezing and breathlessness in asthma and COPD, and before exercise in some people.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Stimulates beta-2 receptors in the airway muscles, making them relax within minutes.

sections.title: Main risks
sections.text: Shaking, fast heartbeat and headache.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text: Needing the reliever often is a sign asthma isn't well controlled. International asthma guidelines (GINA) no longer recommend treating adults and teenagers with a reliever alone.

entries.name: Artemether–lumefantrine
entries.subtitle: Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT) · antimalarial
entries.summary: A WHO-recommended combination treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria.

sections.title: Used for
sections.text: Uncomplicated malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum. Severe malaria needs hospital treatment, usually with injectable artesunate.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Artemether kills parasites quickly; lumefantrine lasts longer in the body and clears the rest. Using two drugs together helps prevent resistance.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text: Taken with food containing some fat, which helps absorption. Caution with other medicines that affect heart rhythm.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text: Partial resistance to artemisinin has been documented in the Greater Mekong region of Southeast Asia, so treatment follows national guidelines.

entries.name: Type 2 diabetes
entries.subtitle: Metabolic disease
entries.summary: The body doesn't respond properly to insulin or doesn't make enough, so blood sugar stays too high.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Thirst, passing urine often, tiredness and blurred vision. Many people have no symptoms for years.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text: Blood tests such as HbA1c or fasting blood glucose.

sections.title: Established treatments
sections.text: Healthy eating, activity and weight management; metformin is usually the first medicine. Other options include SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists and insulin.

sections.title: Why control matters
sections.text: Long-term high blood sugar damages the heart, kidneys, eyes, nerves and feet.

entries.name: High blood pressure
entries.subtitle: Hypertension · cardiovascular
entries.summary: Blood pressure that stays too high. The main preventable cause of stroke and heart disease.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Usually none, which is why regular checks matter.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text: Repeated readings. Guidelines differ on the cut-off: some use 140/90 mmHg, US guidelines use 130/80 mmHg.

sections.title: Established treatments
sections.text: Less salt, activity, weight control and less alcohol. Common medicines: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine, and thiazide diuretics.

entries.name: Asthma
entries.subtitle: Chronic airway disease
entries.summary: Long-term inflammation of the airways that causes attacks of wheezing and breathlessness.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Wheezing, cough, chest tightness and breathlessness, often worse at night or with triggers.

sections.title: Established treatments
sections.text: Inhalers containing a steroid to control inflammation, plus a reliever for symptoms. Treatment is adjusted step by step.

sections.title: Emergency
sections.text: Get urgent help if the reliever doesn't help, or breathing or speaking becomes hard.

entries.name: Tuberculosis (TB)
entries.subtitle: Bacterial infection · Mycobacterium tuberculosis
entries.summary: An airborne infection that usually affects the lungs. It is curable with the full course of treatment.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Cough lasting more than two weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss.

sections.title: Established treatments
sections.text: Several antibiotics taken together for months, usually at least six; WHO also recommends some shorter regimens for certain patients. Finishing treatment prevents drug-resistant TB.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: Early diagnosis and treatment, good ventilation, and the BCG vaccine for young children in many countries.

entries.name: Malaria
entries.subtitle: Parasitic infection spread by mosquitoes
entries.summary: Caused by Plasmodium parasites passed on by Anopheles mosquito bites. Can become severe quickly.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Fever, chills, headache and body aches, usually 1–4 weeks after a bite.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text: A rapid diagnostic test or blood smear. Test before treating.

sections.title: Established treatments
sections.text: Artemisinin combination therapies for uncomplicated falciparum malaria; injectable artesunate for severe malaria.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: Insecticide-treated bed nets, repellents, and in parts of Africa the RTS,S and R21 vaccines for children.

entries.name: Dengue
entries.subtitle: Viral infection spread by Aedes mosquitoes
entries.summary: A common tropical virus infection. Most people recover, but some develop severe dengue.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: High fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, and rash.

sections.title: Warning signs
sections.text: Severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, and drowsiness or restlessness need urgent medical care.

sections.title: Care
sections.text: No specific antiviral. Rest, fluids and paracetamol for fever. Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, which raise bleeding risk.

sections.title: Vaccines
sections.text: Vaccines exist but are recommended only in certain settings and age groups; follow national advice.

entries.name: Pancreatic cancer
entries.subtitle: Cancer · most often pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
entries.summary: Often found late because early symptoms are vague.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Yellowing of skin or eyes, upper belly or back pain, weight loss and new diabetes in some people.

sections.title: Established treatments
sections.text: Surgery when the tumour can be removed; combination chemotherapy such as FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel; olaparib for some people with an inherited BRCA mutation.

sections.title: Under investigation
sections.text: Drugs targeting the KRAS protein, which is altered in most tumours, are being tested in clinical trials.

entries.name: Alzheimer's disease
entries.subtitle: Neurodegenerative disease · most common cause of dementia
entries.summary: A brain disease that slowly damages memory and thinking.

sections.title: Signs
sections.text: Memory loss that disrupts daily life, confusion, and difficulty with planning and language.

sections.title: In the brain
sections.text: Build-up of amyloid plaques and tau tangles, and loss of nerve cells.

sections.title: Treatments
sections.text: Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine and memantine can help symptoms. Lecanemab and donanemab, antibodies that clear amyloid, are approved in some countries for early disease; they need regular brain scans because of a risk of brain swelling or bleeding.

entries.name: Turmeric
entries.subtitle: Curcuma longa · rhizome · spice and Ayurvedic herb
entries.summary: A traditional medicine and everyday spice. Its main compound, curcumin, is widely studied but poorly absorbed.

sections.title: Traditional use
sections.text: Used in Ayurveda for inflammation, digestion and skin.

sections.title: Laboratory research
sections.text: Many studies, but curcumin often gives false positives in lab screens, so these results need caution.

sections.title: Human studies
sections.text: Mostly small trials with mixed results. Not approved as a treatment for any disease.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: Concentrated supplements may raise bleeding risk with blood thinners; liver injury has been reported with some supplements. Cooking amounts are different from supplement doses.

entries.name: Ashwagandha
entries.subtitle: Withania somnifera · root · Ayurvedic herb
entries.summary: A popular Ayurvedic herb marketed for stress and sleep.

sections.title: Traditional use
sections.text: Used in Ayurveda as a 'rasayana' (rejuvenating) herb.

sections.title: Human studies
sections.text: Small, short trials suggest some effect on stress and sleep; larger, longer studies are lacking.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: Cases of liver injury have been reported. Avoid in pregnancy. Some countries have restricted its sale.

entries.name: Ginger
entries.subtitle: Zingiber officinale · rhizome
entries.summary: A spice with some of the better human evidence among herbs, mainly for nausea.

sections.title: Traditional use
sections.text: Used across Asia for nausea, digestion and colds.

sections.title: Human studies
sections.text: Trials and reviews suggest it can ease nausea in pregnancy; evidence for other uses is weaker.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: Large supplement doses may add to the effect of blood thinners.

entries.name: Garlic
entries.subtitle: Allium sativum · bulb
entries.summary: A food with modest effects on blood pressure and cholesterol in some studies.

sections.title: Human studies
sections.text: Reviews of trials report small reductions in blood pressure and cholesterol with garlic supplements; results vary between products.

sections.title: Interactions
sections.text: May raise bleeding risk with blood thinners and lower levels of some HIV medicines, such as saquinavir.

entries.name: Neem
entries.subtitle: Azadirachta indica · leaf, bark, seed oil
entries.summary: A traditional medicinal tree in South Asia, used mostly on the skin and teeth.

sections.title: Traditional use
sections.text: Used in Ayurveda for skin conditions and oral hygiene.

sections.title: Laboratory research
sections.text: Antimicrobial and other effects in lab studies; human evidence is limited.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: Neem oil taken by mouth has caused serious poisoning in young children. Keep it away from children.

entries.name: Max Planck Society
entries.subtitle: Germany · Munich headquarters
entries.summary: Germany's leading basic-research organization, with 84 institutes and research facilities.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Basic research across the natural sciences, life sciences and humanities, including biochemistry, infection biology and molecular medicine.

entries.name: German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ)
entries.subtitle: Germany · Heidelberg · Helmholtz Association
entries.summary: Germany's largest cancer research center, covering the full chain from basic biology to clinical research.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Cancer causes, prevention, diagnosis and new treatments, with patient access through the National Center for Tumor Diseases.

entries.name: Max Delbrück Center (MDC)
entries.subtitle: Germany · Berlin · Helmholtz Association
entries.summary: A center for molecular medicine.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Molecular causes of cardiovascular, metabolic, cancer and neurological diseases.

entries.name: Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI)
entries.subtitle: Germany · Braunschweig · Helmholtz Association
entries.summary: Germany's Helmholtz center for infectious diseases.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Bacteria, viruses, immune responses and new anti-infective drugs.

entries.name: Helmholtz Munich
entries.subtitle: Germany · Munich · Helmholtz Association
entries.summary: A biomedical research center for environmental health.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Diabetes, obesity, allergies and chronic lung diseases, using AI and bioengineering.

entries.name: German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE)
entries.subtitle: Germany · Bonn · Helmholtz Association
entries.summary: Germany's research center for dementia and related diseases.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and other neurodegenerative diseases, from basic research to patient care.

entries.name: German Centers for Health Research (DZG)
entries.subtitle: Germany · national network
entries.summary: Eight centers linking universities, hospitals and institutes to bring research to patients faster.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Cancer (DKTK), diabetes (DZD), heart (DZHK), infection (DZIF), lung (DZL), neurodegeneration (DZNE), mental health (DZPG), child and adolescent health (DZKJ).

entries.name: Paul-Ehrlich-Institut (PEI)
entries.subtitle: Germany · Langen · federal agency
entries.summary: Germany's federal institute for vaccines and biomedicines.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Authorises vaccines, antibodies, blood products and gene and cell therapies; approves clinical trials and monitors side effects.

entries.name: BfArM and DRKS
entries.subtitle: Germany · Bonn and Cologne · federal agency
entries.summary: Germany's Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices, which also runs the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS).

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Medicine and device regulation. DRKS is Germany's WHO-recognised trial registry, mostly for studies led by universities.

entries.name: Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin
entries.subtitle: Germany · Berlin · university hospital
entries.summary: One of Europe's largest university hospitals and a leading German medical faculty.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Clinical research and teaching across medicine.

entries.name: Heidelberg University Hospital
entries.subtitle: Germany · Heidelberg · university hospital
entries.summary: A leading German medical faculty and hospital; Newsweek ranked it 12th in the world in 2026.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Clinical research, cancer, and teaching.

entries.name: Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
entries.subtitle: India · New Delhi
entries.summary: India's apex body for biomedical research.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Biomedical and clinical studies; also runs the Clinical Trials Registry – India (CTRI).

entries.name: CDSCO
entries.subtitle: India · national regulator
entries.summary: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Drug approvals and clinical trial permissions in India.

entries.name: CCRAS
entries.subtitle: India · Ministry of AYUSH
entries.summary: Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Ayurveda research, medicinal plant surveys, monographs and toxicity studies.

entries.name: IMPPAT
entries.subtitle: India · IMSc Chennai · database
entries.summary: A database of Indian medicinal plants and their phytochemicals.

sections.title: Research focus
sections.text: Links plants to their chemical compounds and structures for research.

entries.name: Enzymes
entries.subtitle: Proteins that speed up chemical reactions
entries.summary: Enzymes make the body's chemical reactions happen fast enough to support life. Many medicines work by blocking one.

sections.title: What they do
sections.text: Each enzyme binds specific molecules (substrates) and converts them into products, without being used up itself.

sections.title: Medicines that block enzymes
sections.text: Aspirin and ibuprofen block COX enzymes; statins block HMG-CoA reductase; omeprazole blocks the stomach's proton pump; ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme.

entries.name: Receptors
entries.subtitle: Proteins that receive chemical signals
entries.summary: Receptors sit on or inside cells and respond when a hormone, neurotransmitter or medicine binds to them.

sections.title: Agonists and antagonists
sections.text: An agonist switches a receptor on; an antagonist blocks it. How tightly a molecule binds is its affinity, often given as Kd. The Lab tab shows this with a simple model.

sections.title: Examples
sections.text: Salbutamol activates beta-2 receptors to open the airways; losartan blocks angiotensin receptors to lower blood pressure; ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors to stop nausea.

entries.name: Cytochrome P450 enzymes
entries.subtitle: CYP enzymes · drug metabolism
entries.summary: A family of enzymes, mainly in the liver, that break down a large share of medicines. They cause many drug interactions.

sections.title: How interactions happen
sections.text: If one drug blocks a CYP enzyme, another drug that relies on it can build up to higher levels. If one drug speeds up the enzyme, another can be cleared too fast and work less well.

sections.title: Examples
sections.text: CYP3A4 handles many medicines. Clarithromycin and grapefruit juice can block it; rifampicin and St John's wort can speed it up. People also differ genetically, for example in CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 activity.

entries.name: DNA, RNA and proteins
entries.subtitle: The central dogma of molecular biology
entries.summary: Genes in DNA are copied into RNA, and RNA is read to build proteins. Most drug targets are proteins made this way.

sections.title: The flow
sections.text: DNA → messenger RNA (transcription) → protein (translation). A change in a gene can change the protein and cause disease.

sections.title: In medicine
sections.text: mRNA vaccines deliver instructions for one protein so the immune system learns to recognise it. Many cancer drugs target proteins made by mutated genes, such as KRAS or EGFR.

entries.name: Insulin and blood sugar
entries.subtitle: Hormone signalling and metabolism
entries.summary: Insulin, made by beta cells in the pancreas, lets cells take up glucose from the blood.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: After a meal, insulin binds its receptor on muscle, fat and liver cells, which then take in and store glucose.

sections.title: In diabetes
sections.text: Type 1 diabetes: the body makes little or no insulin. Type 2: cells respond poorly to insulin and, over time, the pancreas makes less.

entries.name: Bayer
entries.subtitle: Germany · Leverkusen
entries.summary: A German life-science company, known for registering the Aspirin trademark in 1899.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Prescription medicines, consumer health and crop science.

entries.name: Boehringer Ingelheim
entries.subtitle: Germany · Ingelheim am Rhein
entries.summary: A family-owned research-based pharmaceutical company.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Human medicines, including respiratory, cardiometabolic and cancer research, and animal health.

entries.name: Merck KGaA
entries.subtitle: Germany · Darmstadt
entries.summary: A science and technology company. It is separate from the US company Merck & Co., which is called MSD outside the US and Canada.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Healthcare, life-science research tools and electronics materials.

entries.name: BioNTech
entries.subtitle: Germany · Mainz
entries.summary: An mRNA biotechnology company that developed a COVID-19 vaccine with Pfizer. It acquired CureVac in December 2025.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: mRNA vaccines and cancer immunotherapies.

entries.name: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries
entries.subtitle: India · Mumbai
entries.summary: One of India's largest pharmaceutical companies.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Generic and specialty medicines.

entries.name: Cipla
entries.subtitle: India · Mumbai
entries.summary: An Indian pharmaceutical company known for low-cost HIV medicines and respiratory inhalers.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Generics, respiratory, HIV and anti-infective medicines.

entries.name: Dr. Reddy's Laboratories
entries.subtitle: India · Hyderabad
entries.summary: A major Indian maker of generic medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Generics, APIs and biosimilars.

entries.name: Serum Institute of India
entries.subtitle: India · Pune
entries.summary: The world's largest vaccine manufacturer by number of doses.

sections.title: Focus
sections.text: Vaccines for childhood immunisation and other diseases.

entries.name: Pulse oximeter
entries.subtitle: Fingertip oxygen and pulse monitor
entries.summary: Shines light through a finger to estimate blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) and pulse rate.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.text: SpO2, the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen, and heart rate.

sections.title: Accuracy limits
sections.text: Cold fingers, poor circulation, movement and nail polish can affect readings. The FDA has warned that pulse oximeters can overestimate oxygen levels in people with darker skin. Use trends and symptoms, not one number.

entries.name: Blood glucose meter
entries.subtitle: Fingerstick and continuous glucose monitoring
entries.summary: Measures blood sugar for people with diabetes. Continuous monitors (CGMs) read glucose under the skin every few minutes.

sections.title: Accuracy standard
sections.text: The ISO 15197 standard requires 95% of readings within ±15 mg/dL of the lab value below 100 mg/dL, or within ±15% above it.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text: CGM readings lag behind blood readings by several minutes, especially when glucose changes quickly.

entries.name: Blood pressure monitor
entries.subtitle: Automatic cuff device
entries.summary: Measures blood pressure. Upper-arm cuff devices are generally preferred over wrist devices.

sections.title: Getting a reliable reading
sections.text: Use a clinically validated device and the right cuff size. Sit quietly for 5 minutes with the arm supported at heart level.

sections.title: Validated devices
sections.text: Independent lists of validated monitors exist, for example STRIDE BP and validatebp.org.

entries.name: Thermometer
entries.subtitle: Digital, ear and forehead
entries.summary: Measures body temperature. Accuracy depends on the type and how it is used.

sections.title: Types
sections.text: Digital thermometers under the tongue, armpit or rectum; infrared ear and forehead devices are faster but more affected by technique and surroundings.

entries.name: ECG (electrocardiogram)
entries.subtitle: Records the heart's electrical activity
entries.summary: Hospitals use 12-lead ECGs; some smartwatches record a single-lead ECG.

sections.title: What it shows
sections.text: Heart rhythm, rate and signs of damage or strain.

sections.title: Wearables
sections.text: Some smartwatch ECG features are FDA-cleared to detect atrial fibrillation. They cannot detect heart attacks and do not replace a 12-lead ECG.
